Henry II. King of England from 1154 to 1189, he initiated the Plantagenet dynasty and through marriage and conquest ruled the vast Angevin Empire. This realm spanned England, parts of Ireland, and over half of modern France. His reign is noted for significant legal reforms that established the foundation of English common law, but is perhaps best remembered for his dramatic conflict with the Church.

His most famous confrontation involved the Archbishop of Canterbury. A bitter dispute between king and archbishop culminated when Thomas Becket was assassinated in Canterbury Cathedral, reportedly after Henry asked in exasperation, "Who will rid me of this turbulent priest?" Earlier in his reign, Henry had issued the Constitutions of Clarendon in 1164, attempting to restrict clerical privileges and submit wayward priests to royal courts. His legal legacy endured through the Assize of Clarendon in 1166, which established grand juries and laid the foundation for the English common law system.

Henry was married to the powerful and wealthy Eleanor of Aquitaine, though this alliance would later prove fraught. Eleanor supported their sons in a major rebellion against him, including the Great Revolt of 1173 to 1174, led by his sons Henry the Young King, Richard, and Geoffrey. His great-grandfather had been William the Conqueror, whose administrative legacy he built upon. His son Richard would become known as the Lionheart, while his surviving son John would ultimately inherit the throne.
